summary: Terfenadine is a second-generation H1-antihistamine that was used for allergic rhinitis and urticaria. It is the prodrug of fexofenadine. Terfenadine was WITHDRAWN from major markets because the parent drug blocks cardiac potassium (hERG/IKr) channels, causing QT prolongation and torsades de pointes - especially when its metabolism (CYP3A4) was inhibited by drugs such as ketoconazole, erythromycin, or grapefruit juice. Its active metabolite fexofenadine carries the antihistamine benefit without the cardiac toxicity and has replaced it.
indications: Historically: symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria (now superseded by fexofenadine; terfenadine is withdrawn)

dosage.n: No longer marketed - withdrawn for cardiac toxicity

dosage.d: Use fexofenadine (the active metabolite), e.g., 180 mg once daily

admin: Terfenadine is no longer available - do not prescribe
Historically the parent drug required intact CYP3A4 metabolism; any CYP3A4 inhibition caused dangerous accumulation
Avoid grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition raised parent terfenadine levels)
If antihistamine therapy is needed, use fexofenadine or another non-cardiotoxic agent
moa: Terfenadine is a selective peripheral H1-receptor antagonist that provides antihistamine relief with minimal sedation. It is a prodrug almost completely metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4 to the active carboxylate metabolite fexofenadine. The PARENT terfenadine (which normally circulates at negligible levels) blocks the cardiac delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKr/hERG), prolonging cardiac repolarization (QT). When CYP3A4 is inhibited or hepatic function impaired, parent drug accumulates, causing QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

absolute: Concomitant CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin)
Known QT prolongation or congenital long QT syndrome
It is withdrawn - effectively contraindicated for all use

preg: Not recommended in pregnancy (formerly Category C); given its withdrawal and cardiac risk, use safer alternatives such as fexofenadine, loratadine, or cetirizine.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding; use a safer, currently marketed antihistamine instead.
renal: Not clinically relevant given withdrawal; fexofenadine (the successor) is partly renally excreted and may need adjustment in renal impairment.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatic impairment - reduced CYP3A4 metabolism causes accumulation of cardiotoxic parent terfenadine and QT prolongation.

major: Azole antifungals (ketoconazole, itraconazole) - CYP3A4 inhibition causing terfenadine accumulation and torsades
Other QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics) - additive QT risk
Grapefruit juice - CYP3A4 inhibition raising parent drug levels
moderate: Protease inhibitors and other strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
interactions.food: Avoid grapefruit juice; otherwise taken without food historically
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive risk and no benefit
interactions.diagnostics: ECG monitoring of QTc was required during use

monitoring: Review for interacting CYP3A4 inhibitors before any use
Because the drug is withdrawn, monitoring is moot - substitute fexofenadine
counsel: This medicine has been withdrawn because it can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems
If you have an old supply, do not use it - ask for a safe alternative such as fexofenadine
Never combine such antihistamines with antifungals, certain antibiotics, or grapefruit juice
Report fainting, palpitations, or dizziness immediately
pk: Parent terfenadine peaks ~1-2 h; active metabolite (fexofenadine) somewhat later
Active metabolite ~16-23 hours; parent normally rapidly metabolized
Was stored at room temperature, protected from moisture (no longer marketed)
pearls: WITHDRAWN worldwide for QT prolongation and torsades de pointes - a landmark example of a drug pulled for cardiac repolarization toxicity
It is the prodrug of fexofenadine; the safe active metabolite replaced it as a 'cleaner' drug
Toxicity occurred when CYP3A4 was inhibited (azoles, macrolides, grapefruit) allowing cardiotoxic parent drug to accumulate
Classic teaching case for hERG/IKr channel blockade and acquired long QT syndrome
missed: Not applicable - terfenadine is withdrawn and should not be in current use; use a currently approved antihistamine such as fexofenadine.
overdose: Overdose causes severe QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, and cardiac arrest, along with anticholinergic effects. Management: continuous cardiac monitoring, correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, give IV magnesium for torsades, supportive care; hemodialysis is not effective because of high protein binding.
